slides.heading: Tournament Winner
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Easy · Arrays
slides.narration: Let's solve Tournament Winner, an easy arrays problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Competitions are [home, away] pairs, results[i]==1 means home won.
A win is worth 3 points; return the team with most points (guaranteed unique).
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Competitions are home, away pairs, results i equals equals 1 means home won. A win is worth 3 points; return the team with most points (guaranteed unique).

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Every match has exactly one winner worth three points, so a running score table is all we need.
slides.narration: Every match has exactly one winner worth three points, so a running score table is all we need.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Brute force: recount every team's points at the end — still O(n)
Simplest optimal: one hash map + running leader
Avoid a second pass by updating the leader on the fly
slides.narration: There isn't a slow brute force here so much as a clumsy one: tally everything, then scan the table for the max. We can do it in a single pass by updating the leader whenever a team's score passes it.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. Keep a hash map of team to points
2. For each match, credit the winner
3. Track the leader as scores change
4. Return the best team
slides.narration: Step by step. First, keep a hash map of team to points. Second, for each match, credit the winner. Third, track the leader as scores change. Fourth, return the best team.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We loop over competitions and results together, pick the winner, add three points in the map, and update the leader if this team now has more points than the current leader.

slides.heading: Complexity
bullets: Time: O(n)
Space: O(k) teams
slides.narration: Time is O of n. Space is O of k teams.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: result = 1 means the HOME team won
Ties can't happen (problem guarantees one winner)
Initialise the leader with an empty team at 0 points
slides.narration: The main pitfall is reading the result backwards: one means the home team won. Initialise the leader as an empty name with zero points so the first winner takes over.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
bullets: Clarify the meaning of result before coding
Follow-up: handle ties (e.g. alphabetical)
Mention O(k) space for k teams
slides.narration: Clarify the result encoding before you start. A natural follow-up is how you'd break ties, for example alphabetically.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Every match has exactly one winner worth three points, so a running score table is all we need.
Complexity: O(n)
